1. The frames show a grid of small squares, which looks like many historical buy-or-rent scenarios. Light squares mean the buyer was ahead after ten years. Dark squares mean the renter was ahead. The data sources are listed as FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. The video labels it "illustrative" and says "US only · history, not a forecast." The idea is that, across past ten-year periods, buying came out ahead in most of them under an assumed rent level.

2. Only the on-screen text changes. Frame 1 shows the grid alone. Frames 2–4 add the caption "rent tag 6%: buyer ahead in 92.2%." Frames 5–6 add "the share moves with the rent you assume," and the first caption fades out. The grid, with its thin dark stripe in the middle, stays essentially the same in every frame.

3. If rent is assumed at 6% of the home's value per year, the buyer was ahead after ten years in about 92.2% of the historical cases, and the renter in the remaining 7.8% or so. The result depends on the rent assumption. A different rent level would change the share.

4. A viewer could take away that buying has usually beaten renting over ten-year horizons, but that the answer depends on how high the rent is compared with the home's price. They should test it with their own local rent and price numbers before deciding. The video says nothing about what to do in particular.

5. The on-screen text suggests part of this. "The share moves with the rent you assume" and "history, not a forecast" point to the caveat that the result depends on assumptions and doesn't predict the future. The advice to check your own rent-to-price numbers is my own conclusion, not something the animation says. The animation doesn't tell anyone to buy or to keep renting.
